name: Hardmaxxing
lead: Hardmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for invasive or medically intensive methods of changing appearance, as opposed to 'softmaxxing', which covers non-invasive practices such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness. [1][2]

The term covers cosmetic and maxillofacial surgery such as rhinoplasty and jaw surgery, injectables such as botulinum toxin, and the use of off-label drugs and peptides. Wikipedia and Grokipedia also list limb-lengthening, hair transplants and steroid use among practices people place under the label, and describe bonesmashing, striking the face, as an extreme and widely criticised fringe idea. [1][3]

A 2026 cross-sectional study of social media discourse about 'dangerous' facial aesthetic trends examined looksmaxxing and its softmaxxing and hardmaxxing practices, including DIY procedures, self-injection and bonesmashing. Surgeons and other experts quoted in coverage warn of complications from unsupervised or overseas procedures and of links with body dysmorphia. [3][4]
infobox: Rhinoplasty, jaw surgery, botulinum toxin, genioplasty, hair transplant, off-label drugs and peptides [1][3]
Surgery and prescription drugs are regulated medical products or procedures; research peptides are generally not approved for these uses

paras: Within looksmaxxing, practices are commonly sorted into soft and hard. Wikipedia describes softmaxxing as non-invasive (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, and also contested practices like mewing) and hardmaxxing as more extreme measures such as off-label substances, extreme dieting, skin whitening and cosmetic surgery. [1]

Grokipedia lists surgical examples as jaw implants, genioplasty, rhinoplasty, hair transplants and limb or clavicle lengthening, as well as steroid use and travel abroad for cheaper procedures, and notes that complication rates at some overseas clinics are reported to be high. [3]

Users on looksmax.org draw up personal hardmaxxing plans that list facial procedures such as maxillary surgeries, rhinoplasty and lip surgery alongside injectables and peptides, often noting that choices differ by individual. [5][6]

A 2026 study in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery used social-listening tools, Google Trends and Instagram engagement metrics to analyse online discussion of dangerous facial aesthetic trends, including looksmaxxing, softmaxxing and hardmaxxing, DIY cosmetic procedures, self-injection and bonesmashing. [4]

Wikipedia reports that surgeons warn of fractures, misalignment and vision damage from bonesmashing, and that a 2025 paper advised physicians to help patients tell safe beauty practices from harmful ones. Commentators have also linked looksmaxxing with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. [1] A 2025 study of a looksmaxxing forum argued that its norms reflect hegemonic masculinity and can harm men's health. [7]
Grokipedia cites reported risks of limb lengthening (infection, nerve damage, long recovery), steroids (hormonal and cardiovascular effects) and unsupervised surgery abroad. [3]

Many forum threads discuss hardmaxxing as a way to approximate favourable bone structure, with questions about how much it can change appearance and what is realistic. Other threads explicitly ask for advice without hardmaxxing, showing that the community treats it as a separate, more serious tier. [5][8]
Grokipedia notes that some looksmaxxing communities have moved away from fatalism toward incremental self-improvement. [3]

No studies of 'hardmaxxing' as a defined practice were found as clinical trials. The individual procedures grouped under it, such as rhinoplasty and orthognathic surgery, have their own clinical literature, and the 2026 social-media study cited above analyses online discussion rather than clinical outcomes. [4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hardmaxxing is discussed as the invasive end of the 'ascension' toolkit, with planning threads, cost questions and debates about how far surgery can mimic good bone structure. [5][6][8]

claims.claim: Surgery and medical procedures can substantially change facial structure.
claims.believers: Posters share plans that combine jaw, maxilla and nose surgery and say procedures should be tailored to each person's features. [5][6]
claims.experts: Surgeons note that structural surgery is an established medical field, but warn about complications and about unrealistic expectations, and clinicians are advised to screen for body dysmorphia. [1]

claims.claim: Peptides and research chemicals add to hardmaxxing results for bones, skin and hair.
claims.believers: One forum list proposes peptides for skin, hair and facial bones, though its author acknowledges possible misinformation. [6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that injectable GHK-Cu is not FDA-regulated and that the evidence for these uses is lacking; no published trials support facial bone effects. [1]

claims.claim: Bonesmashing is a form of hardmaxxing.
claims.believers: Some users joke about or promote it, though Wikipedia calls it an inside joke that is rarely carried out. [1]
claims.experts: Surgeons warn of irregular fractures, asymmetry and vision damage, and Grokipedia says there is no evidence of efficacy. [1][3]

card.summary: Looksmaxxing slang for invasive appearance changes such as surgery, injectables and off-label drugs; established procedures exist, but DIY and fringe variants carry documented risks.
card.note: Covers a wide range from regulated surgery to unregulated peptides and bonesmashing; experts warn of complications and body dysmorphia.

quick.overview:
Hardmaxxing is the invasive end of looksmaxxing: surgery, injectables, drugs and peptides, as opposed to skincare, grooming and fitness (softmaxxing).

The label spans well-established procedures like rhinoplasty and jaw surgery as well as unregulated or fringe practices such as bonesmashing.
quick.mechanism: Surgical methods change bone or soft-tissue shape directly; injectables and drugs act on muscle, skin, hormones or growth pathways. Forum users build personalised plans combining several of these.
quick.risks: Surgeons warn of complications, especially with unsupervised or overseas procedures, fractures and asymmetry from bonesmashing, and hormonal and cardiovascular effects of steroids. Commentators link looksmaxxing with body dysmorphia.
